title: Housing taxes, pension protests and Spain flight cuts

chapters.title: Housing taxes and a strained market

summary:
Spain's housing tax overhaul awaits parliamentary backing as buying and renting remain under pressure. We cover pension protests, upcoming cash payment rules, flight cuts and campaign tax proposals, plus promising melanoma trial results.

Enjoying Spain Daily? Support us: https://buymeacoffee.com/spanified

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Those housing tax changes are already running, but—

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: —Congress's standing committee still has to ratify them.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Already running, but still awaiting backing? That's an odd order.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's quite a starting point for anyone working out their housing costs.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Good morning! It's Sunday, the twenty-fifth of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'm Inna, here with Dima. Today: pensioners' demands and fewer flights into Spain. First, the housing tax overhaul.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Spain's housing tax decree has been in force since October eighth, Expansión reports. Congress's standing committee must still ratify it. The decree changes personal income tax, VAT, property tax and municipal capital gains tax. It revives measures from an earlier decree that failed to win parliamentary backing.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Wait, Dima, does this reach beyond the tax you pay when buying a home?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: It reaches across owning, selling and renting. mhm So people already settled in a home have a reason to follow it.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Four different taxes in one decree, and it's still waiting for a vote in Congress.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That tax debate comes against severe affordability pressure. Madrid home prices rose roughly thirteen percent annually in the third quarter, Expansión reports, although growth slowed. Higher interest rates and affordability pressures are cooling demand. Buying now absorbs sixty-six percent of average household disposable income.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oof. Slower growth sounds comforting until you look at what a household actually has left.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That's the squeeze. Demand is shifting towards better-connected, more affordable areas, rather than everyone suddenly finding Madrid affordable. right

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Housing pressure is also behind a general strike planned for November eleventh, El Diario reports. The employers' association won't challenge the call. The action draws on feminist strikes that extended beyond traditional workplace demands. The planned mobilisation could affect workplaces and services across Spain.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For someone organising work or appointments, that puts the date on the calendar, not just in the political debate.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Right. The earlier feminist strikes also questioned unpaid care and consumption, and the article says this one grows out of similar questions.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: In Barcelona, the rental picture has a different tension. Expansión reports that September rents fell slightly, by zero point seven percent annually, both locally and across Catalonia. Rent caps cover three hundred and two municipalities. Supply and new contracts have also fallen, while Barcelona City Council wants caps extended to commercial premises.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: A small rent drop, but fewer places available. Does that leave someone searching with much to celebrate?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Not much comfort if they can't find a place. exactly The price and the chance of finding a rental both matter.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Buying in Barcelona brings another contrast, according to Expansión. Home prices reached a record of roughly forty-six hundred euros per square metre in the third quarter, up nearly eleven percent annually. First-half sales fell. Buyers are taking longer to complete purchases and securing larger discounts, signs of a slowing market.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Huh. So buyers can negotiate harder even while the headline price keeps climbing?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Those larger discounts suggest more room to negotiate. mhm But a discount from a record price can still leave an expensive home.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Pensions are in the spotlight after yesterday's march in Madrid. El Confidencial reports that pensioners demanded increases matching actual inflation and rejected privatisation. The Government Delegation counted twenty-five thousand participants. Inflation is close to five percent, putting pensions firmly into the debate before the November twenty-ninth election.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's a very direct demand. Keep the buying power, not just raise the amount on paper.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Exactly. A bigger payment doesn't stretch further if everyday prices rise just as quickly.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For larger purchases, adopted EU rules will introduce a ten-thousand-euro cash ceiling from July tenth next year, Heraldo reports. Spain can retain lower limits. Private, non-business transactions and bank deposits are exempt. Businesses covered by anti-money-laundering rules must identify customers paying three thousand euros or more in cash.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Ah, so someone depositing savings at a bank isn't facing the same restriction as someone paying a business?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Bank deposits are exempt. The ceiling also covers linked payments, so splitting a business purchase doesn't get around it.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Travel plans face a squeeze too. Heraldo reports that airlines have removed more than three thousand flights into Spain from November and December schedules. Cirium's figures show that means roughly five hundred and sixty thousand fewer seats. The cuts are attributed to a jet fuel crisis, leaving fewer options before Christmas.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's a lot of missing seats. oh For people travelling between homes, fewer flights can make the dates harder to fit.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And the squeeze can mean higher fares as well. It's availability and cost together, not just a thinner timetable.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: On household taxes, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo outlined campaign proposals yesterday, reports Twenty Minutos. From next year, he would remove VAT on basic foods and electricity while inflation persists. Self-employed people billing under eighty-five thousand euros annually would be exempt from VAT. He also pledged one million homes.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That self-employed threshold catches my eye. Does the proposal measure what someone bills, rather than what they keep?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Annual invoicing, not take-home income. That's the figure a self-employed person would compare with the proposed threshold.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Public finances are under pressure too. El Mundo reports IMF figures for 2018 to 2027 putting Spain's public consumption growth at two point seven percent, against two point one percent for advanced economies. A promised public-sector pay rise would add spending. BBVA Research says meeting fiscal rules is getting harder.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: On interest rates, El País quotes Natixis strategist Mabrouk Chetouane saying French debt tensions could delay a European Central Bank rate rise. He sees no major contagion risk for Spain. His assessment comes ahead of the bank's Thursday, October twenty-ninth meeting.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For anyone with a variable mortgage, that potential delay matters through Euribor, the rate many of those loans follow.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: It does. He's one strategist, though, and he sees Spain as fairly insulated from the French tension.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Finally, some promising news on cancer. El Mundo reports a phase three trial of a personalised messenger RNA vaccine, given with the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab. It cut the risk of relapse or death by forty-two percent in patients with high-risk melanoma, a skin cancer, after surgery. The president of the European oncology society says it's premature to say how far the technology will reach.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Housing runs through today's news: the taxes people pay, the homes they can find, and the pressure on household budgets.
